evidence.finding: Mean service level fell from 88.87% before the incident to 29.16% from 09:15 onward, a 59.71-point decline.
Mean ASA increased from 26.27 seconds to 113.87 seconds, while abandoned calls rose from 2.4 to 30.82 per interval.
Offered calls increased 11.17%, from 70.0 to 77.82 per interval; this was material but not a demand surge.
AHT did not increase: it was essentially flat to slightly lower, moving from 375.96 to 375.05 seconds.
Transfer rate did not increase, declining slightly from 6.18% to 6.05%.
Answered calls fell 30.47% despite higher offered volume, consistent with reduced throughput and sustained queue growth.

primary_root_cause_detail: The incident shows a sustained throughput/capacity failure beginning at 09:15, but center-level performance alone cannot distinguish staffing, routing, queue imbalance, or another operational disruption.
recommended_actions: Inspect interval staffing, adherence, and productive-agent data around 09:15 to identify the source of the capacity loss.
Compare all queues for service-level divergence, staffing imbalance, or localized misrouting.
Review the visible operational event and routing configuration effective at the incident boundary.
Validate actual demand against forecast before changing demand assumptions or staffing plans.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Offered volume rose only 11.17%, which is a moderate increase rather than a surge and is unlikely by itself to explain the 59.71-point service-level collapse.
Post-incident mean AHT decreased by 0.24% rather than increasing.

stakeholder_summary: A real and sustained service-level incident began at 09:15. Demand increased moderately, but AHT and transfers were stable; the dominant pattern was a sharp loss of answered-call throughput. Available center-level evidence is insufficient to identify whether staffing, routing, queue imbalance, or another disruption caused that loss, so the diagnosis remains inconclusive.
